headline: Brazil's Rarest Primate Gets First-Ever Yellow Fever Vaccine
meta_description: In a conservation first, researchers in Brazil vaccinated black-faced lion tamarins against yellow fever, protecting one of the world's rarest primates from di…
summary_short: Three black-faced lion tamarins became the first of their species to receive yellow fever vaccinations in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, a crucial step to protect fewer than…
body:
In July 2026, deep within the restinga shrublands of Paraná state on Brazil's Atlantic coast, three researchers carefully carried cages through the forest to a makeshift tent. Inside were three black-faced lion tamarins—two males and one female—about to make history. Within hours, they would become the first members of their species ever to be vaccinated against yellow fever, a disease that has devastated Brazil's primate populations and poses an existential threat to one of the world's rarest mammals. The vaccination effort, led by the conservation NGO Society for Wildlife Research and Environmental Education (SPVS) and veterinarians including Paula Mangini, represents a turning point for a species with nowhere left to hide. The black-faced lion tamarin, known locally as the caissara lion tamarin, has fewer than 400 individuals surviving in the wild—and crucially, none exist in captivity.

The stakes could hardly be higher. First described by science in 1990, the species was already fragmented by a 6-kilometer canal built in the 1950s that severed its habitat, splitting the population into isolated groups on either side of the waterway. These small, separated communities now face inbreeding depression and reduced genetic diversity. Unlike other lion tamarins, there is no backup population in zoos or research centers—if yellow fever strikes, the species could vanish entirely. Evidence from Superagui Island, where these tamarins live, suggests the virus has already swept through: howler monkeys in the area have disappeared, and these animals are extremely susceptible to yellow fever.

The vaccination initiative emerged as a lifeline. By providing biological defense against one of the most serious threats to Brazil's primates, researchers are buying time for the species while longer-term habitat restoration and population monitoring continue. It is a reminder that the smallest, most overlooked creatures sometimes require the most innovative solutions.
quick_facts: Fewer than 400 black-faced lion tamarins remain in the wild, with zero in captivity
Vaccinations took place in Paraná state's Atlantic Forest restinga in July 2026
A 6-kilometer canal built in 1950 fragmented the species' habitat into isolated groups
No captive population exists to repopulate if disease wipes out the wild population
